steps.text:
I read both files in full: `parser.py` is 533 lines and `formatting.py` is 320. I also ran a short script to check a few behaviours I describe below. They follow the same pattern as `core.py`: they don't know about Click's concepts (types, defaults, envvars, prompts, help text). Each does one mechanical job, and `core.py` feeds them input and interprets their output.

# `parser.py`: turning tokens into raw values

It's a cut-down copy of the stdlib's `optparse`. Everything is private, and the old public names (`OptionParser`, `Option`, `split_opt`, …) are still reachable through a deprecated module `__getattr__` (line 503).

## Pieces

- **`_split_opt(opt)`** (111): splits an option into prefix and name: `"--foo"` → `("--", "foo")`, `"-f"` → `("-", "f")`, `"foo"` → `("", "foo")`. `core.py` uses it to derive option names, `Group.resolve_command` uses it to decide whether an unknown command name looks like an option, and `formatting.join_options` uses it too.
- **`_normalize_opt(opt, ctx)`** (120): runs `ctx.token_normalize_func` on the name part and keeps the prefix. It's applied both when options are registered and when tokens are matched.
- **`_unpack_args(args, nargs_spec)`** (51): hands positional tokens out to arguments according to their `nargs`. Any slot that can't be filled gets `UNSET`. A single `nargs=-1` argument takes the leftover tokens: arguments after it are filled from the end of the list, so `SRC... DST` works. A second `-1` raises `TypeError`.
- **`_Option`** (127): the parser-side record for one `core.Option`. It splits the spellings into short options (one-character name with a one-character prefix) and long options, and collects their prefixes. `process()` applies the action:

  | Action | Effect on `state.opts[dest]` |
  |---|---|
  | `store` | set to the value |
  | `store_const` | set to `const` |
  | `append` | append the value to a list |
  | `append_const` | append `const` to a list |
  | `count` | increment by 1 |

  Each call also appends the `core.Option` object to `state.order`.
- **`_Argument`** (185): the parser-side record for a `core.Argument`. For `nargs>1`, if every slot is `UNSET` the whole value becomes `UNSET`; if only some are, it raises `BadArgumentUsage`. An empty tuple (`nargs=-1` with nothing left) also becomes `UNSET`.
- **`_ParsingState`** (216): `opts` (dest → raw value), `largs` (positionals seen so far), `rargs` (tokens not yet read) and `order` (core param objects in the order they appeared).

## `_OptionParser` (224)

- **`__init__(ctx)`**: copies `allow_interspersed_args` and `ignore_unknown_options` from the context. Starts with `_opt_prefixes = {"-", "--"}`, and options can add more (e.g. `/`, `+`).
- **`add_option` / `add_argument`**: only called from `core.Option.add_to_parser` and `core.Argument.add_to_parser`. That `core` method is where Click's concepts get translated into parser actions:
  - `multiple` → `append`
  - `count` → `count`
  - flags → the `*_const` actions, with `const=flag_activation_value`
  - `--x/--no-x` → two registrations with `const=True` and `const=False`
- **`parse_args(args)`** → `(opts, largs, order)`. Runs in two passes:
  1. **`_process_args_for_options`**: reads tokens left to right.
     - `--` stops option processing; everything after it counts as positional.
     - A token that starts with a known prefix goes to `_process_opts`.
     - Any other token goes to `largs`. If interspersed args are disabled (the `Group` default), the parser instead stops at the first such token and pushes it back. That's how a group leaves `subcmd --sub-opts…` untouched for the child command.
  2. **`_process_args_for_args`**: `_unpack_args(largs + rargs, …)`. Whatever no argument consumes ends up in the returned leftovers.

  Under `ctx.resilient_parsing`, a `UsageError` from either pass is swallowed and the partial state is returned. If the error came from the options pass, positional arguments are never assigned.
- **`_process_opts`**: splits on `=` and tries a long-option match first, so `-foo` can be a long option. If that fails and the token doesn't start with a two-character prefix like `--`, it retries as a group of short options. Otherwise it raises `NoSuchOption`, or keeps the token in `largs` when unknown options are ignored.
- **`_match_long_opt`**: puts an `=value` back in front of `rargs`. Raises `BadOptionUsage` if a flag gets a value. Includes `possibilities` in the error so it can suggest similar names.
- **`_match_short_opt`**: handles grouped short options like `-abc`. When an option that takes a value is found, the rest of the token becomes its value (`-oval`). With `ignore_unknown_options`, unknown characters are rejoined into one token that goes to `largs`.
- **`_get_value_from_state`**: reads `nargs` tokens. This is where the **`FLAG_NEEDS_VALUE`** sentinel is created: if `option.obj._flag_needs_value` is set and there are no tokens left, or the next token looks like an option, the parser returns the sentinel instead of failing. This reads a private attribute of `core.Option` directly, so the parser can't work with an option object that isn't a `core.Option`.

Behaviours I confirmed by running them:
- `-o=val` gives `o='=val'`. The `=` split only applies to long options. For short options, the full token is processed as a group, so `=val` becomes the value. optparse does the same.
- `a -o x b` gives `rest=('a','b')` (interspersed positionals).
- `-- -o x` gives `rest=('-o','x')`.

# `formatting.py`: writing help into a buffer

- **`HelpFormatter`** (110): writes help text into an in-memory buffer (`getvalue()` joins it).
  - **Width:** `width`, otherwise `FORCED_WIDTH`, otherwise `max(min(terminal_columns, max_width) - 2, 50)`, where `max_width` defaults to 80. `CliRunner` sets `FORCED_WIDTH = 80` (`testing.py:439`) so test output doesn't depend on the terminal.
  - **Indentation:** `indent()` / `dedent()` change `current_indent` by `indent_increment` (default 2). The `indentation()` context manager wraps that, and `section(name)` adds a blank line, a `Name:` heading, and indentation for its contents.
  - **`write_usage(prog, args, prefix)`**: `Usage: prog args`, with the args wrapped so continuation lines line up under them. If the prefix is too long to leave 20 columns, the args go on the next line instead.
  - **`write_paragraph()`**: writes a blank line, but only if something has already been written.
  - **`write_text(text)`**: wraps at the current indent and keeps paragraph breaks.
  - **`write_dl(rows, col_max=30, col_spacing=2)`**: the two-column table used for options, arguments and commands. If the first column is wider than `col_max`, the description moves to the next line. A row with an empty description prints just the term, which is how undocumented arguments appear in the "Positional arguments" section.
- **`wrap_text(...)`** (31): wraps text with Click's own `_textwrap.TextWrapper`, measuring ANSI-aware width with `term_len`. In paragraph mode, it keeps each paragraph's indentation, and a paragraph whose first line is just `\b` is not rewrapped.
- **`measure_table` / `iter_rows`**: compute column widths and pad short rows for `write_dl`.
- **`join_options(opts)`**: sorts option spellings by prefix length (so `-v, --verbose`) and reports whether any used `/`.

# How the three fit together

## Parsing: one `Command.parse_args` call

```
Command.make_context ─► Context(...)                 # settings inherited / from Command
  └─ Command.parse_args(ctx, args)
       ├─ make_parser(ctx): _OptionParser(ctx)        # copies interspersed/unknown flags
       │     └─ for p in get_params(ctx): p.add_to_parser(parser, ctx)
       │           Option   → parser.add_option(obj=self, action=…, const=…, nargs=…)
       │           Argument → parser.add_argument(obj=self, nargs=…)
       ├─ opts, leftovers, order = parser.parse_args(args)
       │     opts:  {name: raw str | tuple | list | const | count | UNSET | FLAG_NEEDS_VALUE}
       │     order: core Parameter objects in CLI order
       ├─ for p in iter_params_for_processing(order, params):   # eager first, then CLI order
       │     p.handle_parse_result(ctx, opts, leftovers)
       │        consume_value: opts[name], else envvar, else default_map, else default
       │                       (Option: FLAG_NEEDS_VALUE → prompt or flag_activation_value)
       │        process_value: type_cast_value → required check → user callback
       │        then arbitration writes ctx.params[name] + ParameterSource
       ├─ UNSET → None in ctx.params; extra leftovers → "unexpected extra argument"
       └─ ctx.args = leftovers; ctx._opt_prefixes |= parser._opt_prefixes
```

How the work is split:

- **The parser only produces raw values.** It doesn't check types, required params, defaults or envvars. Two sentinels carry its "no value" signals to `core`: `UNSET` means the parser saw nothing, which tells `consume_value` to try the other sources. `FLAG_NEEDS_VALUE` means the option appeared without a value, and `Option.consume_value` turns that into a prompt or the activation value.
- **`order` controls callback order.** The parser records the `core.Parameter` objects themselves, not their names, and `iter_params_for_processing` compares them by identity. That's why `Command.get_help_option` must cache its option: building a new one each time would break the comparison against `order`.
- **`dest` is the param's `name`.** Several options with the same `dest` (feature switches) all write into the same `opts` key. The parser keeps whichever came last. `Parameter.handle_parse_result` then decides which param owns `ctx.params[name]`, using the `ParameterSource` ordering.
- **How groups use the parser:** a `Group` has `allow_interspersed_args=False`, so the parser stops at the subcommand name and returns it and everything after it as leftovers. `Group.parse_args` splits those into `_protected_args` (the name) and `ctx.args`. `Group.invoke` then calls `cmd.make_context(name, args, parent=ctx)`, which runs a new parser for the child. In chain mode, each child is created with `allow_extra_args=True` and `allow_interspersed_args=False`, so its leftovers become the next command's input.
- **`ctx._opt_prefixes`** collects the parser's prefixes down the context chain. Shell completion uses it to decide whether an incomplete token looks like an option (`shell_completion.py:668`).
- **Errors:** the parser raises `NoSuchOption`, `BadOptionUsage` and `BadArgumentUsage` with `ctx` attached. `Command.main` catches them as `ClickException` and calls `show()`.

## Help: `get_help` delegates layout to the formatter

`Command.get_help` → `ctx.make_formatter()` builds a `ctx.formatter_class(width=ctx.terminal_width, max_width=ctx.max_content_width)`, which `format_help` fills:

| core.py method | Formatter call |
|---|---|
| `format_usage` → `collect_usage_pieces` + `ctx.command_path` | `write_usage(prog, " ".join(pieces))` |
| `format_help_text` (cut at `\f`, add deprecated label) | `write_paragraph()` + `indentation()` + `write_text` |
| `format_arguments` (`Argument.get_help_record` → `(metavar, help or "")`) | `section("Positional arguments")` + `write_dl` |
| `format_options` (`Option.get_help_record` → `(get_help_spec, help + [extras])`) | `section("Options")` + `write_dl` |
| `Group.format_commands` (`get_short_help_str(limit)`) | `section("Commands")` + `write_dl` |
| `format_epilog` | `write_paragraph()` + `indentation()` + `write_text` |

- `core` produces the content: the help strings, metavars, the `[env var: …; default: …; required]` extras, and the left-column spec built with `join_options`. The formatter only handles layout, indentation and wrapping.
- Help text uses two control characters, one in each module: **`\f`** is handled in `core.format_help_text` (everything after it is dropped), and **`\b`** is handled in `formatting.wrap_text` (don't rewrap this block).
- `Group.format_commands` estimates the room for each command's short help as `formatter.width - 6 - longest_name`, and passes that as the limit to `get_short_help_str`.
- To customise help, the extension points are `Context.formatter_class` (subclass `HelpFormatter`) and the `format_*` methods on `Command`/`Group`.

## Small issues I noticed

1. **`write_dl` doesn't subtract `current_indent` when sizing the description column** (formatting.py:261): it uses `self.width - first_col - 2`. The fixed `- 2` happens to match one section level, so normal help output fits. Deeper nesting overflows: in my check, a formatter with `width=60` produced 62-character lines at indent 6. That only affects custom formatters that nest sections.
2. **The parser reads `option.obj._flag_needs_value` directly** (parser.py:438, 454). Anyone still using the deprecated `parser.OptionParser` with their own objects as `obj` will hit an `AttributeError` when the option is missing a value.
3. **The width floor can exceed `max_width`:** `max(min(cols, max_width) - 2, 50)` ignores a `max_content_width` below 52. That's probably intended, but it's undocumented.
4. **Resilient parsing can skip positionals:** if the options pass raises, positional arguments are never assigned. That only matters for completion, where `UNSET` values are acceptable anyway.

Nothing was changed, and I didn't run the test suite, just the one-off check script.

steps.text:
I read both files in full: `decorators.py` is 627 lines and `types.py` is 1,437. I also ran a short script to check the pipeline end to end. It turned up one real bug, in `BoolParamType`; details are at the end.

# `decorators.py` in brief

- **`option()` / `argument()`** (352 / 324): each builds the param object right away, as `cls(param_decls, **attrs)`, and stores it with `_param_memo`. If the target is still a function, the param goes on a `f.__click_params__` list. If it's already a `Command`, it's appended to `cmd.params`.
- **`command()`** (168): takes `f.__click_params__`, deletes it, and appends it **reversed** after any `params=` you passed explicitly. Decorators run from the bottom up, so reversing restores the top-to-bottom order you wrote. It also uses `f.__doc__` as the default `help`, and derives the name from the function: lowercase, `_` → `-`, with `_command`/`_cmd`/`_group`/`_grp` suffixes removed. Then it calls `cls(name=…, callback=f, params=…, **attrs)`. **`group()`** is the same with `cls=Group`.
- **Prebuilt options**: these are all ordinary `option()` calls with defaults filled in:
  - `help_option`: eager flag, `expose_value=False`, callback prints `ctx.get_help()` and calls `ctx.exit()`.
  - `version_option`: eager. Detects the package name from the caller's frame globals, then resolves the version with `importlib.metadata`, falling back to `packages_distributions()`.
  - `custom_version_option`: like `version_option`, but your callback builds the string.
  - `confirmation_option`: prompts, and the callback aborts on "no".
  - `password_option`: prompt plus hidden input plus confirmation.

  All of them use **callbacks** and **`is_eager`**, which are the two hooks in `process_value`/`iter_params_for_processing`.
- **Passing objects to the callback**: `pass_context`, `pass_obj`, `make_pass_decorator(type, ensure)` and `pass_meta_key` wrap the callback and read `get_current_context()` when it's called. They don't touch the params.

# `types.py` in brief

- **`ParamType`** (65): the base class. `__call__(value, param, ctx)` returns `None` for `None` and otherwise calls `convert`. The default `convert` returns the value unchanged; `fail()` raises `BadParameter`. Other hooks: `split_envvar_value` (whitespace by default; `File`/`Path` use `os.pathsep`), `get_metavar`, `get_missing_message`, `shell_complete`, `to_info_dict`. Class attributes `is_composite`/`arity` tell `Parameter` how many tokens one value uses.
- **Built-in types**:

  | Type | What `convert` does |
  |---|---|
  | `StringParamType` (`STRING`) | decodes bytes (argv encoding, then filesystem encoding, then utf-8 with replacement), otherwise `str(value)` |
  | `UnprocessedParamType` (`UNPROCESSED`) | returns the value unchanged |
  | `IntParamType`/`FloatParamType` (`INT`/`FLOAT`) | `_number_class(value)` |
  | `IntRange`/`FloatRange` | range check through `_NumberRangeBase`, optionally clamping. Open float bounds can't be clamped. `_describe_range` provides the `[0<=x<=10]` help text |
  | `BoolParamType` (`BOOL`) | `str_to_bool` lookup in the `bool_states` table |
  | `UUIDParameterType` (`UUID`) | parses a UUID |
  | `DateTime` | tries each format in order |
  | `Choice` | normalizes the input, matches it against normalized choices, and returns the **original** choice object (enums work too) |
  | `File` | opens the file and registers `ctx.call_on_close` to close it; returns a `_LazyFile` for write mode |
  | `Path` | stat, existence and permission checks, then `coerce_path_result` to `path_type` |
  | `Tuple` | composite: `arity = len(types)`, converts each item with its own type |
  | `FuncParamType` | wraps a plain callable such as `type=int`-like functions; only `ValueError` is turned into `BadParameter` |

- **`convert_type(ty, default)`** (1356): turns the `type=` argument into a `ParamType`:
  - With no explicit `type`, `_guess_type` infers it from the default. A tuple/list default gives the type of its first item, or a `Tuple` type if that item is itself a sequence.
  - `str`/`int`/`float`/`bool` map to the singletons. A tuple of types gives `Tuple`.
  - A guessed type that isn't one of the basic four falls back to `STRING`. An explicit unknown callable gets wrapped in `FuncParamType`.
  - Passing an uninstantiated `ParamType` class asserts.

# How a value gets from the decorator to `process_value`

Running example (I ran this one; `X` is the envvar):

```python
@click.command()
@click.option("--x", type=click.IntRange(0, 10, clamp=True), envvar="X",
              callback=lambda ctx, p, v: v * 2)
@click.argument("pts", nargs=-1, type=float)
def c3(x, pts): ...
```

## 1. Definition time: decorators build the `Parameter` objects

```
@argument("pts", nargs=-1, type=float)      runs first (bottom-up)
   └─ Argument(("pts",), nargs=-1, type=float) → f.__click_params__ = [pts]
@option("--x", type=IntRange(...), ...)
   └─ Option(("--x",), ...)                   → f.__click_params__ = [pts, x]
@command()
   └─ params = reversed(...) = [x, pts]       → Command(name="c3", callback=f, params=[x, pts])
```

Everything about the type is fixed inside `Parameter.__init__` (core.py:2335):

- `self.type = types.convert_type(type, default)`. Here `float` maps to `FLOAT`, and the `IntRange` instance is used as is. With no `type` and no `default`, `default` is the `UNSET` sentinel, so `_guess_type` returns `type(UNSET)`, which is not one of the basic four, so the result is `STRING`.
- `nargs` comes from `type.arity` when the type is composite, so a `Tuple` sets `nargs` for you. A mismatch raises in `__debug__` mode.
- For options, `Option.__init__` then runs `_pick_type`, which overrides the type for flags (`BOOL`, or a type guessed from `flag_value`) and counts (`IntRange(min=0)`). That's why a flag's type comes from `flag_value` rather than `default`.

At this point nothing has been converted. `default` is stored raw, and may be a callable or `UNSET`.

## 2. Parse time: the parser produces raw values

As covered last time, `Command.parse_args` → `make_parser` → `_OptionParser.parse_args` returns `opts = {"x": "99", "pts": ("1", "2.5")}`, plus `order`. The values are still raw strings or tuples of strings. Anything the parser didn't see is absent, or `UNSET` for arguments.

## 3. `handle_parse_result` → `consume_value`: pick a raw value and record its source

`Parameter.consume_value` (core.py:2528) returns the first available source:

| Source | Raw shape | `ParameterSource` |
|---|---|---|
| `opts[name]` from the parser | str, tuple, list, const, or `FLAG_NEEDS_VALUE` | `COMMANDLINE` |
| `value_from_envvar` | str, or `type.split_envvar_value(...)` when `nargs != 1` (Option: also `multiple`, batched for `multiple`+`nargs>1`, and bool reading for non-bool flags) | `ENVIRONMENT` |
| `ctx.lookup_default(name)` | whatever the map holds; strings are split when `nargs != 1` | `DEFAULT_MAP` |
| `get_default(ctx)` | `self.default` (called if callable; Option applies `_resolve_lazy_default`) | `DEFAULT` |
| nothing | `UNSET` | `DEFAULT` |

`Option.consume_value` then resolves `FLAG_NEEDS_VALUE`, or prompts. `prompt_for_value` passes `value_proc=lambda x: self.process_value(ctx, x)` to `termui.prompt`, so **prompted input goes through the full pipeline inside the prompt loop**, and a `BadParameter` makes it ask again.

**The type is the only thing that turns raw strings into typed values.** Envvars and default-map entries are never converted before this point; they're just split. That's why `convert` must accept both strings and values that already have the right type: a default of `5` and the command-line string `"5"` go through the same `INT.convert`.

## 4. `process_value`: convert, check required, run the callback

`Parameter.process_value` (core.py:2650):

```
value is UNSET?
 ├─ yes → stays UNSET (or () if multiple / nargs=-1); type is never called
 └─ no  → type_cast_value(ctx, value)
            None → () for multiple/nargs=-1, else None
            pick convert() by shape:
              nargs==1 or composite → self.type(value, self, ctx)
              nargs==-1             → tuple(self.type(x) for x in iter(value))
              nargs==N              → length check, then tuple(self.type(x) ...)
            multiple → tuple(convert(x) for x in iter(value))   # outer loop
              └─ ParamType.__call__ → None passes through, else convert()
                   └─ e.g. IntRange: int("99") = 99 → clamp → 10
required and value_is_missing(value)?  → MissingParameter
callback?  → value = callback(ctx, param, value)       # UNSET shown as None
```

`Option.process_value` adds one shortcut before this: an unset, non-required bool flag becomes `False`, and its callback is called directly.

Back in `handle_parse_result`, errors are tagged by `augment_usage_errors(ctx, param)`. `ParamType.fail` raises `BadParameter` with `ctx`/`param` set when it has them, and the wrapper fills them in when it doesn't (e.g. a `FuncParamType`). The result then goes through the feature-switch arbitration into `ctx.params[name]`. Finally, `Command.parse_args` turns any remaining `UNSET` into `None`, and `Command.invoke` calls `callback(**ctx.params)`.

What my run printed:
- `--x 99 1 2.5` → `x=20 pts=(1.0, 2.5) src=COMMANDLINE`. The string `"99"` went through `IntRange`: converted to int, clamped to 10, then doubled by the callback. Each argument token went through `FLOAT`.
- `X=3` in the environment → `x=6 src=ENVIRONMENT`. The envvar string took exactly the same path.
- No input → my callback crashed on `None * 2`. That's correct behaviour, not a bug: when nothing supplies a value, it stays `UNSET`, the type is never called, and the callback receives `None`. **A param callback must handle `None`.**

## Where to customise each step

| Stage | Hook |
|---|---|
| Declaration | `cls=` on `option`/`argument`/`command`, `Group.command_class` |
| Picking a type | `type=` (a `ParamType`, a Python type or a callable), or `default=` for inference |
| Splitting envvar/default-map strings | `ParamType.envvar_list_splitter` / `split_envvar_value` |
| Conversion | subclass `ParamType.convert`, calling `self.fail(...)` on bad input |
| Validation after conversion | `callback=(ctx, param, value)` |
| Order | `is_eager=True` |

# Things worth knowing

**1. Bug: `BoolParamType` crashes on non-string, non-bool input** (types.py:868). `str_to_bool` calls `value.strip()` on anything that isn't a `bool`. So `type=bool, default=1`, or a default map loaded from JSON/TOML with `{"b": 0}`, raises a raw `AttributeError` instead of converting the value or raising `BadParameter`. I reproduced both:

```
bool default=1       -> AttributeError("'int' object has no attribute 'strip'")
bool default_map 0   -> AttributeError("'int' object has no attribute 'strip'")
```

This also breaks the `ParamType` contract (docstring at types.py:66–80) that `convert` accepts compatible Python values. A fix would map `0`/`1` ints, or `str()` non-strings before the lookup, and fail cleanly on anything else. I can do that with a test if you want.

**2. Gotcha: a callable default makes the type `STRING`.** `@option("--n", default=lambda: 5)` gives `n == '5'` (a string). `_guess_type` sees a function and falls back to `STRING`. Pass `type=int` explicitly with dynamic defaults.

**3. `FuncParamType` only catches `ValueError`.** A `type=` callable that raises `TypeError` or anything else produces a traceback instead of a usage error.

**4. Minor inconsistency in `Path`:** the `executable` check uses `value` (types.py:1224) while every other check uses `rv`, the resolved path. Both normally point to the same file, so it's harmless in practice.

Nothing was modified. The only things I ran were the probe scripts, not the test suite.

steps.text:
I ran the full suite with `-v`, keeping the defaults from `pyproject.toml` (`addopts = "-m 'not stress'"`, warnings treated as errors). **Everything passed: 2,098 passed, 25 skipped, 1 xfailed, 31,000 deselected, in 3.75 s.**

There are 2,124 test names, too many to paste here. The complete verbose output is saved at `/tmp/click-pytest-v.log` (2,133 lines). Notes on the run:

- **The 31,000 deselected** are the `@pytest.mark.stress` tests, in `test_stream_lifecycle.py` (around line 486) and `test_utils/test_echo_via_pager.py:228`. They're tiny cases repeated thousands of times to catch race conditions, which is why the count is so high. Tox runs them by clearing `addopts` (`pyproject.toml:183`).
- **The 25 skips** are platform-only: 22 Windows `getchar`/editor tests in `test_termui.py`, one Windows fd test in `test_testing.py`, and `test_path_surrogates`, which depends on the filesystem encoding.
- **The 1 xfail** is `test_chain.py::test_group_chaining`, marked `@pytest.mark.xfail` without a reason.

## How the tests are organised

The layout is flat and mostly follows the source modules. There's one shared fixture, `runner`, a `CliRunner` defined in `tests/conftest.py`. Almost every test builds a small command inline and calls `runner.invoke(cli, args, env=…, default_map=…)`, then checks the output or exit code.

| Area | Files (selected test count) |
|---|---|
| `core.py` params | **`test_options.py` (664)**, `test_arguments.py` (116), `test_defaults.py` (46) |
| Commands, groups, context | `test_basic.py` (109, end-to-end basics), `test_commands.py` (103), `test_chain.py` (16), `test_context.py` (30), `test_command_decorators.py` (9), `test_custom_classes.py` (6), `test_normalization.py` (3), `test_abort_interrupt.py` (8) |
| `parser.py` / `formatting.py` | `test_parser.py` (7), `test_formatting.py` (37) |
| `types.py` | `tests/test_types/` has one file per type: `test_convert_type` (30), `test_IntRange` (14), `test_Path` (9), `test_FloatRange` (8), plus Choice/File/FuncParamType/ParamType |
| Introspection and deprecations | `test_info_dict.py` (38), `test_deprecations.py` (28) |
| Terminal I/O, utilities | `test_termui.py` (282), `test_compat.py` (175), `test_stream_lifecycle.py` (24), `tests/test_utils/` (style, pager, prompt, echo, …), `test_testing.py` (45), `test_shell_completion.py` (58) |
| Static typing | `tests/typing/*.py` are files for a type checker to check, not pytest tests, so they don't appear in the run |

## Where option behaviour is tested

Nearly all of it is in `tests/test_options.py`: 104 distinct test functions, 664 cases once parametrized. It's grouped roughly by theme, in file order:

- **Declaration and parsing (lines 21–200):** prefixes, unknown options with "did you mean" suggestions, counting, nargs/tuple/multiple, deprecation.
- **Defaults and multiple (263–800):** good and bad defaults for `multiple`, inferring the type from container defaults, dynamic defaults in help, `show_default` with `default_map`.
- **Validation, required, choices (878–1065):** custom callbacks, `test_callback_validates_prompt`, required options and flags, case-insensitive `Choice`.
- **Custom classes (1092–1227):** including `test_option_custom_class_can_override_type_cast_value_and_never_sees_unset`.
- **Flags (1227–1900):** aliases, `show_default` for flags, optional-value options (the `FLAG_NEEDS_VALUE` path), `flag_value` type inference, invalid flag definitions.
- **Custom `flag_value` types (2124–2685):** objects that are left as-is instead of stringified, callable flag values that must not be called.
- **Feature-switch arbitration, issue #3403 (2685–3626):** `test_bool_flag_pair_default`, a family of `test_*flag_group_competition*` tests covering command line, envvar, `default_map`, four-way groups, repeated flags and `ParameterSource`, plus the name-sharing warnings.

Related option tests elsewhere: `test_defaults.py` (default/`default_map` interplay), `test_basic.py` (end-to-end flags/choices), `test_formatting.py` (help rendering), `test_info_dict.py` (introspected `default`/`flag_value`), and `test_utils/test_prompt.py` plus `test_termui.py` for prompts.

## Where env var behaviour is tested

**`test_options.py` has the most coverage, with 58 references:**

| Test | Line | What it covers |
|---|---|---|
| `test_empty_envvar` | 434 | empty string counts as unset |
| `test_multiple_envvar` / `test_envvar_container_type` | 445 / 458 | splitting for `multiple` and containers |
| `test_boolean_flag_envvar` | 560 | 45 cases of bool-flag envvar readings |
| `test_boolean_envvar_bad_values` | 599 | 17 unrecognised values |
| `test_nargs_envvar` | 816 | `nargs` splitting |
| `test_toupper_envvar_prefix` | 805 | `auto_envvar_prefix` gets upper-cased |
| `test_show_envvar*` | 841–863 | help display, including the auto prefix and dashes in command names |
| `test_missing_envvar` | 998 | `show_envvar` in the missing-param error |
| `test_envvar_string_flag_value` | 1803 | 71 cases of non-bool flag envvars, i.e. `Option.value_from_envvar`'s flag_value/bool reading |
| `test_bool_flag_group_competition_with_envvar` | 2969 | envvar vs default in arbitration |
| `test_flag_group_competition_envvar_prefix_and_unset_default_map` | 3594 | auto prefix in arbitration |

Elsewhere:
- `test_arguments.py:181` and `:201`: envvars on arguments with `nargs`, and that the envvar is used only when no CLI values were given.
- `test_context.py:754`: `auto_envvar_prefix` passed through `context_settings`.
- `test_defaults.py:351`: `test_flask_debug_env_not_stomped_by_default_flag`.
- `test_info_dict.py` and `test_shell_completion.py`: a few incidental references.
- `test_testing.py:341`: `CliRunner`'s own `env=` handling.

## Two gaps relevant to earlier findings

- **The `BoolParamType` crash I found last time has no test.** Nothing in the suite gives a `type=bool` option an int default, or a `default_map` with `0`/`1`. That's why the suite is green despite the bug. The natural places for a regression test are next to `test_boolean_envvar_bad_values` in `test_options.py`, or in a new `tests/test_types/test_Bool.py`.
- **Auto-envvar prefix nesting** is only tested lightly: the upper-casing, help display and the one context test. I didn't find a test that checks the nested `PARENT_SUB_OPTION` name a subcommand's option gets when reading its value.

I didn't change any repo files. The only side effect is the usual `tests/__pycache__` bytecode.

All the error cases exit with code 2, as they should. Only the hint text is wrong.

**Where the bugs are (in `src/click/core.py`):**
- **Error hint, `Option.get_error_hint` (line 3271):** it builds the hint as `f" (env var: '{self.envvar}')"` whenever `self.envvar is not None`. A list gets printed with its Python repr, and `''`/`[]` get through because they aren't `None`. The help path already joins list entries with `", "`; the error path doesn't.
- **Help line, `Option.get_help_extra` (lines 3439–3454):** it only checks `envvar is None`. So `''` becomes `("",)` and `[]` becomes `()`, and both render as the empty `env var: `.
- **The two paths also don't match the runtime lookup.** `Parameter.resolve_envvar_value` uses `if not self.envvar`, so at runtime `''` and `[]` count as "no envvar" and Click falls back to the auto-prefix name. From reading the code (I haven't run this), if a context has `auto_envvar_prefix` set and the option has `envvar=''`, help would show `[env var: ]` while the value is actually read from `PREFIX_UNITS`. A fix should probably make all three use the same truthiness check, and give the error hint the same join/auto-prefix logic as the help line.

steps.text:
There's one root cause: **three pieces of code each work out "which env var(s) does this option use?" on their own, with different rules.** Only one of them is used to actually read the value. The other two, the help line and the error hint, each have their own version, and both versions are wrong in different ways.

## The three places

**1. Runtime lookup: the behaviour the other two should describe.** `Parameter.resolve_envvar_value` (`core.py:2741`) and `Option.resolve_envvar_value` (`core.py:3580–3586`):

```python
2741        if not self.envvar:          # truthiness: None, "" and [] all mean "no envvar"
2742            return None
...
3585        if self.allow_from_autoenv and ctx.auto_envvar_prefix is not None and self.name:
3586            envvar = f"{ctx.auto_envvar_prefix}_{self.name.upper()}"   # then fall back to auto-prefix
```

So at runtime, `''` and `[]` are treated as unset. A list is read entry by entry, and the auto-prefix name is the fallback.

**2. Help line, `Option.get_help_extra` (`core.py:3440–3454`).** The checks use `is None` instead of truthiness:

```python
3440            envvar = self.envvar
3442            if envvar is None:                       # '' and [] are not None → auto-prefix fallback skipped
...
3450            if envvar is not None:                   # '' and [] are not None → recorded anyway
3451                if isinstance(envvar, str):
3452                    extra["envvars"] = (envvar,)     # ''  → ("",)
3453                else:
3454                    extra["envvars"] = tuple(str(d) for d in envvar)   # []  → ()
```

`get_help_record` then renders this at line 3421: `_("env var: {var}").format(var=", ".join(extra["envvars"]))`. Joining `("",)` or `()` gives an empty string, which produces **`[env var: ]`**. Lists work here only because line 3454 iterates over them and line 3421 joins them.

**3. Error hint, `Option.get_error_hint` (`core.py:3273–3274`).** It has the same `is None` problem, and it doesn't handle lists or the auto prefix at all:

```python
3273        if self.show_envvar and self.envvar is not None:     # '' and [] pass
3274            result += f" (env var: '{self.envvar}')"         # raw f-string interpolation
```

`f"{self.envvar}"` calls `str()` on whatever is stored there:
- `['WEATHER_UNITS', 'UNITS']` becomes the list repr, so you get **`(env var: '['WEATHER_UNITS', 'UNITS']')`**
- `[]` becomes `'[]'`, so **`(env var: '[]')`**
- `''` becomes nothing, so **`(env var: '')`**

The hint is used for `BadParameter` (`exceptions.py:150`) and `MissingParameter` (`exceptions.py:188`), so both kinds of error message are affected.

## A fourth symptom with the same cause, confirmed

I ran the auto-prefix case I'd only described from reading last time, using a command with `auto_envvar_prefix="WEATHER"` and `WEATHER_UNITS` set:

| `envvar=` | Help | Value actually read from | Error hint |
|---|---|---|---|
| `''` | `[env var: ]` | `WEATHER_UNITS` (`units='metric'`) | `(env var: '')` |
| `[]` | `[env var: ]` | `WEATHER_UNITS` | `(env var: '[]')` |
| `None` | `[env var: WEATHER_UNITS]` | `WEATHER_UNITS` | **no env var hint at all** |

So for `''` and `[]`, the help line and error hint describe an env var that doesn't exist, while the value really comes from `WEATHER_UNITS`. For the normal `None` + auto-prefix case, the help line is right, but the error hint leaves out the env var the bad value came from. That's because line 3273 only checks `self.envvar` and never looks at the auto prefix.

## Summary

| Question | Runtime (2741/3585) | Help (3442/3450) | Error hint (3273) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Is `''`/`[]` "no envvar"? | yes (`not self.envvar`) | **no** (`is None`) | **no** (`is not None`) |
| Auto-prefix fallback? | yes | yes, but skipped for `''`/`[]` | **never** |
| List formatting | iterates over entries | `", ".join` | **`str(list)`** |

The fix is to compute the effective env var names once, e.g. an `Option` helper that uses `if not self.envvar`, normalises to a tuple and applies the auto-prefix fallback. Then both `get_help_extra` and `get_error_hint` would format that tuple with `", ".join(...)`. If none are left, both would leave the env var out instead of printing an empty one.

I haven't changed any repo files. The extra check ran from the scratch directory.

steps.text:
**Fix: format `show_envvar` hints correctly for lists and empty values**

With `show_envvar=True`, Click was showing env vars badly in two ways:

- **Lists in error messages:** a list or tuple `envvar` showed up in error messages as a Python repr, e.g. `(env var: '['A', 'B']')`.
- **Empty values:** `envvar=""` or `envvar=[]` showed an empty `[env var: ]` in help and an empty hint in errors.

The cause is that the help and error paths checked `is None`, while the runtime lookup checks truthiness. The error path also never joined list entries.

What changed in `Option` (`src/click/core.py`, +8 −4):
- **`get_error_hint`** joins list or tuple entries with `", "`, as the help already did. It skips empty values.
- **`get_help_extra`** checks truthiness instead of `is None`. With an `auto_envvar_prefix`, an empty `envvar` now shows the prefixed name, which is the env var actually read at runtime.

There are 9 new test cases in `tests/test_options.py` plus a `CHANGES.md` entry. The full suite passes (2,107 passed).

**Things to flag for review:**
1. **Visible help change:** `envvar=""` or `[]` with an `auto_envvar_prefix` now shows `[env var: PREFIX_NAME]` instead of `[env var: ]`. This is intended, since it matches what the runtime reads, but it is a change in help output.
2. **Not fixed:** a list that contains an empty name (`[""]`, `["", "B"]`) still shows the empty entry.
3. **Not fixed, existing gaps:**
   - The error hint never names an auto-prefix env var, even when the help does.
   - When both `envvar` and an auto prefix are set, the runtime falls back to the prefixed name, but the help lists only the explicit one. I spotted this by reading the code and haven't tested it.
   - Both are better handled as separate issues.
4. **Before merging:**
   - The changelog entry needs an `{issue}`/`{pr}` reference.
   - ruff and mypy/pyright weren't available, so lint and type checks haven't run.

147	def iter_params_for_processing(
148	    invocation_order: cabc.Sequence[Parameter],
149	    declaration_order: cabc.Sequence[Parameter],
150	) -> list[Parameter]:
151	    """Returns all declared parameters in the order they should be processed.
152	
153	    The declared parameters are re-shuffled depending on the order in which
154	    they were invoked, as well as the eagerness of each parameters.
155	
156	    The invocation order takes precedence over the declaration order. I.e. the
157	    order in which the user provided them to the CLI is respected.
158	
159	    This behavior and its effect on callback evaluation is detailed at:
160	    https://click.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/advanced/#callback-evaluation-order
161	    """
162	
163	    def sort_key(item: Parameter) -> tuple[bool, float]:
164	        try:
165	            idx: float = invocation_order.index(item)
166	        except ValueError:
167	            idx = float("inf")
168	
169	        return not item.is_eager, idx
170	
171	    return sorted(declaration_order, key=sort_key)

862	    def invoke(
863	        self, callback: Command | t.Callable[..., V], /, *args: t.Any, **kwargs: t.Any
864	    ) -> t.Any | V:
865	        """Invokes a command callback in exactly the way it expects.  There
866	        are two ways to invoke this method:
867	
868	        1.  the first argument can be a callback and all other arguments and
869	            keyword arguments are forwarded directly to the function.
870	        2.  the first argument is a click command object.  In that case all
871	            arguments are forwarded as well but proper click parameters
872	            (options and click arguments) must be keyword arguments and Click
873	            will fill in defaults.
874	
875	        .. versionchanged:: 8.0
876	            All ``kwargs`` are tracked in :attr:`params` so they will be
877	            passed if :meth:`forward` is called at multiple levels.
878	
879	        .. versionchanged:: 3.2
880	            A new context is created, and missing arguments use default values.
881	        """
882	        if isinstance(callback, Command):
883	            other_cmd = callback
884	
885	            if other_cmd.callback is None:
886	                raise TypeError(
887	                    "The given command does not have a callback that can be invoked."
888	                )
889	            else:
890	                callback = t.cast("t.Callable[..., V]", other_cmd.callback)
891	
892	            ctx = self._make_sub_context(other_cmd)
893	
894	            for param in other_cmd.params:
895	                if param.name not in kwargs and param.expose_value:
896	                    default_value = param.get_default(ctx)
897	                    # We explicitly hide the :attr:`UNSET` value to the user, as we
898	                    # choose to make it an implementation detail. And because ``invoke``
899	                    # has been designed as part of Click public API, we return ``None``
900	                    # instead. Refs:
901	                    # https://github.com/pallets/click/issues/3066
902	                    # https://github.com/pallets/click/issues/3065
903	                    # https://github.com/pallets/click/pull/3068
904	                    if default_value is UNSET:
905	                        default_value = None
906	                    kwargs[param.name] = param.type_cast_value(ctx, default_value)
907	
908	            # Track all kwargs as params, so that forward() will pass
909	            # them on in subsequent calls.
910	            ctx.params.update(kwargs)
911	        else:
912	            ctx = self
913	
914	        with augment_usage_errors(self), ctx:
915	            return callback(*args, **kwargs)

1371	    def parse_args(self, ctx: Context, args: list[str]) -> list[str]:

1375	        parser = self.make_parser(ctx)
1376	        opts, args, param_order = parser.parse_args(args=args)
1377	
1378	        for param in iter_params_for_processing(param_order, self.get_params(ctx)):
1379	            _, args = param.handle_parse_result(ctx, opts, args)
1380	
1381	        # We now have all parameters' values into `ctx.params`, but the data may contain
1382	        # the `UNSET` sentinel.
1383	        # Convert `UNSET` to `None` to ensure that the user doesn't see `UNSET`.
1384	        #
1385	        # Waiting until after the initial parse to convert allows us to treat `UNSET`
1386	        # more like a missing value when multiple params use the same name.

1391	            if value is UNSET:

1398	                    "Got unexpected extra arguments ({args})",
1399	                    len(args),
1400	                ).format(args=" ".join(map(str, args)))
1401	            )

1404	        ctx._opt_prefixes.update(parser._opt_prefixes)

1423	    def shell_complete(self, ctx: Context, incomplete: str) -> list[CompletionItem]:
1424	        """Return a list of completions for the incomplete value. Looks
1425	        at the names of options and chained multi-commands.
1426	
1427	        Any command could be part of a chained multi-command, so sibling
1428	        commands are valid at any point during command completion.

1431	        :param incomplete: Value being completed. May be empty.
1432	
1433	        .. versionadded:: 8.0
1434	        """
1435	        from click.shell_completion import CompletionItem
1436	
1437	        results: list[CompletionItem] = []
1438	
1439	        if incomplete and not incomplete[0].isalnum():
1440	            for param in self.get_params(ctx):
1441	                if (
1442	                    not isinstance(param, Option)
1443	                    or param.hidden
1444	                    or (
1445	                        not param.multiple
1446	                        and ctx.get_parameter_source(param.name)
1447	                        is ParameterSource.COMMANDLINE

1449	                ):
1450	                    continue
1451	
1452	                results.extend(
1453	                    CompletionItem(name, help=param.help)
1454	                    for name in [*param.opts, *param.secondary_opts]
1455	                    if name.startswith(incomplete)
1456	                )
1457	
1458	        while ctx.parent is not None:

1460	
1461	            if isinstance(ctx.command, Group) and ctx.command.chain:

1463	                    CompletionItem(name, help=command.get_short_help_str())
1464	                    for name, command in _complete_visible_commands(ctx, incomplete)

1505	        a :class:`Command`.

81	            nargs = nargs_spec.pop()
82	
83	        if nargs == 1:
84	            rv.append(_fetch(args))
85	        elif nargs > 1:
86	            x: list[str | T_UNSET] = [_fetch(args) for _ in range(nargs)]
87	
88	            # If we're reversed, we're pulling in the arguments in reverse,
89	            # so we need to turn them around.
90	            if spos is not None:
91	                x.reverse()

93	            rv.append(tuple(x))
94	        elif nargs < 0:
95	            if spos is not None:
96	                raise TypeError("Cannot have two nargs < 0")

98	            spos = len(rv)
99	            rv.append(UNSET)
100	
101	    # spos is the position of the wildcard (star).  If it's not `None`,
102	    # we fill it with the remainder.
103	    if spos is not None:
104	        rv[spos] = tuple(args)
105	        args = []
106	        rv[spos + 1 :] = reversed(rv[spos + 1 :])

108	    return tuple(rv), list(args)

127	class _Option:
128	    def __init__(
129	        self,
130	        obj: CoreOption,
131	        opts: cabc.Sequence[str],
132	        dest: str | None,
133	        action: str | None = None,
134	        nargs: int = 1,
135	        const: t.Any | None = None,

146	                        option=opt

153	                self._long_opts.append(opt)

171	            state.opts[self.dest] = value  # type: ignore
172	        elif self.action == "store_const":
173	            state.opts[self.dest] = self.const  # type: ignore
174	        elif self.action == "append":
175	            state.opts.setdefault(self.dest, []).append(value)  # type: ignore
176	        elif self.action == "append_const":
177	            state.opts.setdefault(self.dest, []).append(self.const)  # type: ignore
178	        elif self.action == "count":
179	            state.opts[self.dest] = state.opts.get(self.dest, 0) + 1  # type: ignore

224	class _OptionParser:
225	    """The option parser is an internal class that is ultimately used to
226	    parse options and arguments.  It's modelled after optparse and brings
227	    a similar but vastly simplified API.  It should generally not be used
228	    directly as the high level Click classes wrap it for you.
229	
230	    It's not nearly as extensible as optparse or argparse as it does not
231	    implement features that are implemented on a higher level (such as
232	    types or defaults).
233	
234	    :param ctx: optionally the :class:`~click.Context` where this parser
235	                should go with.
236	
237	    .. deprecated:: 8.2
238	        Will be removed in Click 9.0.
239	    """
240	
241	    def __init__(self, ctx: Context | None = None) -> None:
242	        #: The :class:`~click.Context` for this parser.  This might be
243	        #: `None` for some advanced use cases.
244	        self.ctx = ctx
245	        #: This controls how the parser deals with interspersed arguments.
246	        #: If this is set to `False`, the parser will stop on the first
247	        #: non-option.  Click uses this to implement nested subcommands
248	        #: safely.
249	        self.allow_interspersed_args: bool = True
250	        #: This tells the parser how to deal with unknown options.  By
251	        #: default it will error out (which is sensible), but there is a
252	        #: second mode where it will ignore it and continue processing
253	        #: after shifting all the unknown options into the resulting args.
254	        self.ignore_unknown_options: bool = False
255	
256	        if ctx is not None:
257	            self.allow_interspersed_args = ctx.allow_interspersed_args
258	            self.ignore_unknown_options = ctx.ignore_unknown_options
259	
260	        self._short_opt: dict[str, _Option] = {}
261	        self._long_opt: dict[str, _Option] = {}
262	        self._opt_prefixes = {"-", "--"}
263	        self._args: list[_Argument] = []
264	
265	    def add_option(
266	        self,
267	        obj: CoreOption,
268	        opts: cabc.Sequence[str],
269	        dest: str | None,
270	        action: str | None = None,
271	        nargs: int = 1,
272	        const: t.Any | None = None,
273	    ) -> None:
274	        """Adds a new option named `dest` to the parser.  The destination
275	        is not inferred (unlike with optparse) and needs to be explicitly
276	        provided.  Action can be any of ``store``, ``store_const``,
277	        ``append``, ``append_const`` or ``count``.
278	
279	        The `obj` can be used to identify the option in the order list
280	        that is returned from the parser.
281	        """
282	        opts = [_normalize_opt(opt, self.ctx) for opt in opts]
283	        option = _Option(obj, opts, dest, action=action, nargs=nargs, const=const)
284	        self._opt_prefixes.update(option.prefixes)
285	        for opt in option._short_opts:
286	            self._short_opt[opt] = option
287	        for opt in option._long_opts:
288	            self._long_opt[opt] = option
289	
290	    def add_argument(self, obj: CoreArgument, dest: str | None, nargs: int = 1) -> None:
291	        """Adds a positional argument named `dest` to the parser.
292	
293	        The `obj` can be used to identify the option in the order list
294	        that is returned from the parser.
295	        """
296	        self._args.append(_Argument(obj, dest=dest, nargs=nargs))
297	
298	    def parse_args(
299	        self, args: list[str]
300	    ) -> tuple[dict[str, t.Any], list[str], list[CoreParameter]]:
301	        """Parses positional arguments and returns ``(values, args, order)``
302	        for the parsed options and arguments as well as the leftover
303	        arguments if there are any.  The order is a list of objects as they
304	        appear on the command line.  If arguments appear multiple times they
305	        will be memorized multiple times as well.
306	        """
307	        state = _ParsingState(args)
308	        try:
309	            self._process_args_for_options(state)
310	            self._process_args_for_args(state)
311	        except UsageError:
312	            if self.ctx is None or not self.ctx.resilient_parsing:
313	                raise
314	        return state.opts, state.largs, state.order
315	
316	    def _process_args_for_args(self, state: _ParsingState) -> None:
317	        pargs, args = _unpack_args(
318	            state.largs + state.rargs, [x.nargs for x in self._args]
319	        )
320	
321	        for idx, arg in enumerate(self._args):
322	            arg.process(pargs[idx], state)
323	
324	        state.largs = args
325	        state.rargs = []
326	
327	    def _process_args_for_options(self, state: _ParsingState) -> None:
328	        while state.rargs:
329	            arg = state.rargs.pop(0)
330	            arglen = len(arg)
331	            # Double dashes always handled explicitly regardless of what
332	            # prefixes are valid.
333	            if arg == "--":
334	                return
335	            elif arg[:1] in self._opt_prefixes and arglen > 1:
336	                self._process_opts(arg, state)
337	            elif self.allow_interspersed_args:
338	                state.largs.append(arg)
339	            else:
340	                state.rargs.insert(0, arg)
341	                return
342	
343	        # Say this is the original argument list:
344	        # [arg0, arg1, ..., arg(i-1), arg(i), arg(i+1), ..., arg(N-1)]
345	        #                            ^
346	        # (we are about to process arg(i)).
347	        #
348	        # Then rargs is [arg(i), ..., arg(N-1)] and largs is a *subset* of
349	        # [arg0, ..., arg(i-1)] (any options and their arguments will have
350	        # been removed from largs).
351	        #
352	        # The while loop will usually consume 1 or more arguments per pass.
353	        # If it consumes 1 (eg. arg is an option that takes no arguments),
354	        # then after _process_arg() is done the situation is:
355	        #
356	        #   largs = subset of [arg0, ..., arg(i)]
357	        #   rargs = [arg(i+1), ..., arg(N-1)]
358	        #
359	        # If allow_interspersed_args is false, largs will always be
360	        # *empty* -- still a subset of [arg0, ..., arg(i-1)], but
361	        # not a very interesting subset!
362	
363	    def _match_long_opt(
364	        self, opt: str, explicit_value: str | None, state: _ParsingState
365	    ) -> None:
366	        if opt not in self._long_opt:
367	            raise NoSuchOption(opt, possibilities=self._long_opt, ctx=self.ctx)
368	
369	        option = self._long_opt[opt]
370	        if option.takes_value:
371	            # At this point it's safe to modify rargs by injecting the
372	            # explicit value, because no exception is raised in this
373	            # branch.  This means that the inserted value will be fully
374	            # consumed.
375	            if explicit_value is not None:
376	                state.rargs.insert(0, explicit_value)
377	
378	            value = self._get_value_from_state(opt, option, state)
379	
380	        elif explicit_value is not None:
381	            raise BadOptionUsage(
382	                opt, _("Option {name!r} does not take a value.").format(name=opt)
383	            )
384	
385	        else:
386	            value = UNSET
387	
388	        option.process(value, state)
389	
390	    def _match_short_opt(self, arg: str, state: _ParsingState) -> None:
391	        stop = False
392	        i = 1
393	        prefix = arg[0]
394	        unknown_options = []
395	
396	        for ch in arg[1:]:
397	            opt = _normalize_opt(f"{prefix}{ch}", self.ctx)
398	            option = self._short_opt.get(opt)
399	            i += 1
400	
401	            if not option:
402	                if self.ignore_unknown_options:
403	                    unknown_options.append(ch)
404	                    continue
405	                raise NoSuchOption(opt, ctx=self.ctx)
406	            if option.takes_value:
407	                # Any characters left in arg?  Pretend they're the
408	                # next arg, and stop consuming characters of arg.
409	                if i < len(arg):
410	                    state.rargs.insert(0, arg[i:])
411	                    stop = True
412	
413	                value = self._get_value_from_state(opt, option, state)
414	
415	            else:
416	                value = UNSET
417	
418	            option.process(value, state)
419	
420	            if stop:
421	                break
422	
423	        # If we got any unknown options we recombine the string of the
424	        # remaining options and re-attach the prefix, then report that
425	        # to the state as new large.  This way there is basic combinatorics
426	        # that can be achieved while still ignoring unknown arguments.
427	        if self.ignore_unknown_options and unknown_options:
428	            state.largs.append(f"{prefix}{''.join(unknown_options)}")
429	
430	    def _get_value_from_state(
431	        self, option_name: str, option: _Option, state: _ParsingState
432	    ) -> str | cabc.Sequence[str] | T_UNSET | T_FLAG_NEEDS_VALUE:
433	        nargs = option.nargs
434	
435	        value: str | cabc.Sequence[str] | T_UNSET | T_FLAG_NEEDS_VALUE
436	
437	        if len(state.rargs) < nargs:
438	            if option.obj._flag_needs_value:
439	                # Option allows omitting the value.
440	                value = FLAG_NEEDS_VALUE
441	            else:
442	                raise BadOptionUsage(
443	                    option_name,
444	                    ngettext(
445	                        "Option {name!r} requires an argument.",
446	                        "Option {name!r} requires {nargs} arguments.",
447	                        nargs,
448	                    ).format(name=option_name, nargs=nargs),
449	                )
450	        elif nargs == 1:
451	            next_rarg = state.rargs[0]
452	
453	            if (
454	                option.obj._flag_needs_value
455	                and isinstance(next_rarg, str)
456	                and next_rarg[:1] in self._opt_prefixes
457	                and len(next_rarg) > 1
458	            ):
459	                # The next arg looks like the start of an option, don't
460	                # use it as the value if omitting the value is allowed.
461	                value = FLAG_NEEDS_VALUE
462	            else:
463	                value = state.rargs.pop(0)
464	        else:
465	            value = tuple(state.rargs[:nargs])
466	            del state.rargs[:nargs]
467	
468	        return value
469	
470	    def _process_opts(self, arg: str, state: _ParsingState) -> None:
471	        explicit_value = None
472	        # Long option handling happens in two parts.  The first part is
473	        # supporting explicitly attached values.  In any case, we will try
474	        # to long match the option first.
475	        if "=" in arg:
476	            long_opt, explicit_value = arg.split("=", 1)
477	        else:
478	            long_opt = arg
479	        norm_long_opt = _normalize_opt(long_opt, self.ctx)
480	
481	        # At this point we will match the (assumed) long option through
482	        # the long option matching code.  Note that this allows options
483	        # like "-foo" to be matched as long options.
484	        try:
485	            self._match_long_opt(norm_long_opt, explicit_value, state)
486	        except NoSuchOption:
487	            # At this point the long option matching failed, and we need
488	            # to try with short options.  However there is a special rule
489	            # which says, that if we have a two character options prefix
490	            # (applies to "--foo" for instance), we do not dispatch to the
491	            # short option code and will instead raise the no option
492	            # error.
493	            if arg[:2] not in self._opt_prefixes:
494	                self._match_short_opt(arg, state)
495	                return
496	
497	            if not self.ignore_unknown_options:
498	                raise
499	
500	            state.largs.append(arg)

39	    assumes that it operates on a single paragraph of text but if the
40	    `preserve_paragraphs` parameter is provided it will intelligently
41	    handle paragraphs (defined by two empty lines).
42

44	    line containing the ``\\b`` character (``\\x08``) to indicate that
45	    no rewrapping should happen in that block.

48	    :param width: the maximum width for the text.

50	                           first line as a string.
51	    :param subsequent_indent: the indent string that should be placed on
52	                              each consecutive line.
53	    :param preserve_paragraphs: if this flag is set then the wrapping will
54	                                intelligently handle paragraphs.

57	        Width is measured in visible characters. ANSI escape sequences in
58	        ``text``, ``initial_indent``, or ``subsequent_indent`` no longer
59	        count toward the width budget, so styled input wraps based on what
60	        the user sees instead of raw byte length.
61	    """
62	    from ._textwrap import TextWrapper
63	
64	    text = text.expandtabs()
65	    wrapper = TextWrapper(
66	        width,
67	        initial_indent=initial_indent,
68	        subsequent_indent=subsequent_indent,
69	        replace_whitespace=False,
70	    )
71	    if not preserve_paragraphs:

74	    p: list[tuple[int, bool, str]] = []

76	    indent = None

79	        if not buf:
80	            return

82	            p.append((indent or 0, True, "\n".join(buf[1:])))
83	        else:

85	        del buf[:]

1	## Version 8.5.1
2	
3	Unreleased
4	
5	- Fix `copy.deepcopy()` and `pickle` on a `Parameter`, `Option` or `Command`. {pr}`3805`
6	- A `KeyboardInterrupt` arriving while `Command.main()` reports an abort or an error,
7	  or while it exits, no longer escapes as an unhandled traceback. The command still
8	  exits with the intended code; only the message may be lost. {issue}`3802`
9	- Add {meth}`Option.get_help_spec`, which returns the option's left help
10	  column even when the option is hidden. {meth}`Option.get_help_record` still
11	  returns `None` for hidden options, so help screens are unchanged. {pr}`3821`
12	- The `Positional arguments` help section lists every argument of the command,
13	  not only the documented ones. An argument with no `help` gets an empty
14	  description, the same way an option with no `help` does. {pr}`3860`
15	- {meth}`Argument.get_help_record` always returns a tuple. It used to return
16	  `None` for an argument with no `help`. {pr}`3860`
17	- Document which types are inferred from `default`, and what an unrecognized
18	  `type` callable does to a command-line value. {issue}`3036` {pr}`3808`
19	- `path_type` narrows the converted value's type for `convert` and `prompt`.
20	  {issue}`3822` {pr}`3858`
21	- {class}`Parameter` accepts a new `help` argument and {class}`Option` and {class}`Argument`
22	  inherits it. {meth}`Parameter.to_info_dict` now reports `help` for every kind of parameter.
23	  {pr}`3861`
24	- A command's short help no longer stops at an abbreviation such as `vs.` or `e.g.`
25	  inside the first sentence. A period ends the sentence only when it closes the text
26	  or the next word does not start in lowercase. {pr}`3865`
27	
28	## Version 8.5.0
29	
30	Released 2026-08-24
31	
32	- Add built-in shell completion support for PowerShell (Windows PowerShell
33	  5.1+ and pwsh 7+) alongside the existing `bash`, `zsh`, and `fish`
34	  completers. Use `_FOO_BAR_COMPLETE=powershell_source foo-bar` to generate
35	  the completion script. {issue}`2672` {pr}`3637`
36	- Supported versions of Windows enable ANSI terminal styles by default.
37	  Colorama is no longer a dependency and is not used. {issue}`2986` {pr}`3505`
38	- {class}`Argument` accepts a `help` parameter, and help output includes
39	  a `Positional arguments` section when argument help is available. {issue}`2983` {pr}`3473`
40	- `confirm()` and `prompt()` strip ANSI color and style codes from the
41	  prompt when the output stream does not support them, matching `echo()`.
42	  This stripping was lost in `8.4.0` when {pr}`2969` began writing the
43	  prompt with `input()` directly. {issue}`3572` {pr}`3653`
44	- Fix test failures when using pytest >= 9.1. {pr}`3656`
45	- {class}`Path` with `allow_dash=True` no longer triggers a `BytesWarning`,
46	  an error under `python -bb`, when checking a value against the `-`
47	  convention. {issue}`2877` {pr}`3642`
48	- Add {func}`custom_version_option`, a `--version` option whose output is
49	  produced by a callback, covering cases {func}`version_option` intentionally
50	  does not. The feature set of {func}`version_option` is now frozen; see
51	  [discussion #3527](https://github.com/pallets/click/discussions/3527). {pr}`3581`
52	- `style()` and `secho()` no longer silently drop the 256-color index `0`
53	  (black) passed as `fg` or `bg`, and now validate color arguments. Invalid
54	  colors raise a `ValueError` instead of a `TypeError`. {pr}`3677`
55	- The automatic help option stores its value under the reserved name
56	  `_click_default_help` instead of `help`, so a parameter named `help` no
57	  longer breaks parsing. The new name is visible in
58	  {meth}`Command.to_info_dict` output. Parameters that overwrite each other's
59	  value trigger a warning: an argument sharing its name with another
60	  parameter, or any parameter claiming the reserved name. Options may still
61	  share a name to compete for the same value (feature switches).
62	  {issue}`2819` {pr}`3678`
63	- `unstyle` and the ANSI handling behind help-text wrapping now strip the full
64	  CSI escape-sequence grammar. {pr}`3681`
65	- Streamline `Option` flag handling: the flag-kind, type, lazy-default and
66	  validation steps in `Option.__init__` move into focused helpers, and
67	  `flag_value` and `default` keep their unset sentinel at construction
68	  (resolved lazily on read) so `is UNSET` reliably tells a user-supplied value
69	  from an auto-derived one. Runtime behavior is unchanged, but
70	  {meth}`Parameter.to_info_dict` now resolves `default=True` on a feature
71	  switch to its `flag_value`, matching what the function receives at call
72	  time. {pr}`3641`
73	- {func}`get_binary_stream` and {func}`get_text_stream` are deprecated and
74	  will be removed in Click 9.0. {issue}`3481` {pr}`3695`
75	- The following `click.utils` names were never intentionally public and are
76	  now private (`_`-prefixed). The old names remain available with a
77	  `DeprecationWarning` until Click 9.0: `LazyFile`, `KeepOpenFile`,
78	  `make_default_short_help`, `PacifyFlushWrapper`, and `safecall`.
79	  {issue}`3099` {pr}`3695`
80	- Deprecate {meth}`CliRunner.isolated_filesystem`. It relies on
81	  {func}`os.chdir`, which mutates process-global state and is not
82	  thread-safe. The helper predates Python 3 and modern pytest: use a
83	  temporary directory ({class}`tempfile.TemporaryDirectory` or pytest's
84	  `tmp_path` fixture) with absolute paths instead. For running tests in
85	  parallel, use process-based isolation (such as `pytest-xdist`) rather
86	  than threads, since {meth}`CliRunner.invoke` also redirects the
87	  process-global standard streams. {issue}`3501` {issue}`3700` {pr}`3704`
88	- `prompt()` is now generically typed and returns the type produced by
89	  `type`, `value_proc`, or a matching `default` instead of `Any`.
90	  {class}`ParamType` takes a second optional type parameter describing the
91	  input value it accepts (`ParamType[int, str]` for a type converting
92	  strings to integers), defaulting to `Any`. {pr}`3407`
93	- {meth}`Command.get_help_option_names` returns the help option names in the
94	  order they were declared. {pr}`3728`
95	- {func}`get_pager_file` yields a text stream on Windows again. The temporary
96	  file backend opened its file in binary mode, so writing a `str` to the pager
97	  raised `TypeError: a bytes-like object is required, not 'str'`, and the
98	  `color` argument was ignored on that path. Regression introduced in `8.4.0`
99	  by {pr}`1572`. {issue}`3731` {issue}`3732` {issue}`3740` {pr}`3739`
100	- {func}`progressbar` settles on its final position when `update_min_steps`
101	  does not divide the total. Steps below that threshold are applied when the
102	  bar finishes, so `show_pos` renders `20/20` rather than the last multiple
103	  it reached. {issue}`3571` {pr}`3769`
104	- An error raised while writing to the pager no longer gets replaced by
105	  `PermissionError: [WinError 32]` on Windows. The temporary file backend
106	  unlinked its file without closing it first, and Windows refuses to remove a
107	  file the process still holds open, so the cleanup failure masked the real
108	  exception. {issue}`3731` {pr}`3764`
109	- The temporary file the pager writes to on Windows is opened with the encoding
110	  {func}`get_pager_file` picked for the output stream, and with
111	  `errors="replace"` to match the pipe backend. Any text stdout can encode
112	  reaches the pager.
113	- The temporary file pager backend forwards any parameters the user set in
114	  `PAGER` to the pager command instead of silently dropping them. On Windows,
115	  `PAGER="less -R"` now invokes `less -R` on the temporary file rather than
116	  bare `less`. {pr}`3777`
117	- Improve raw mode detection by parsing the option tokens. {issue}`3416`
118	  {pr}`3777`
119	- {func}`edit` accepts `os.PathLike` values for `filename`, in addition to
120	  strings. {issue}`2869` {pr}`3781`
121

    ("empty-str", ""),
    ("empty-list", []),
]


def make_cli(envvar):
    @click.command()
    @click.option(
        "--units", envvar=envvar, show_envvar=True, type=int, help="Units."
    )
    def cli(units):
        pass

## Version 8.5.1

Unreleased

- Fix `copy.deepcopy()` and `pickle` on a `Parameter`, `Option` or `Command`. {pr}`3805`
- A `KeyboardInterrupt` arriving while `Command.main()` reports an abort or an error,
  or while it exits, no longer escapes as an unhandled traceback. The command still
  exits with the intended code; only the message may be lost. {issue}`3802`
- Add {meth}`Option.get_help_spec`, which returns the option's left help
  column even when the option is hidden. {meth}`Option.get_help_record` still
  returns `None` for hidden options, so help screens are unchanged. {pr}`3821`
- The `Positional arguments` help section lists every argument of the command,
  not only the documented ones. An argument with no `help` gets an empty
  description, the same way an option with no `help` does. {pr}`3860`
- {meth}`Argument.get_help_record` always returns a tuple. It used to return
  `None` for an argument with no `help`. {pr}`3860`
- Document which types are inferred from `default`, and what an unrecognized
  `type` callable does to a command-line value. {issue}`3036` {pr}`3808`
- `path_type` narrows the converted value's type for `convert` and `prompt`.
  {issue}`3822` {pr}`3858`

608	### Value sources
609	
610	Click resolves the value of every option from the following
611	sources, in order of decreasing precedence:
612	
613	1. **command line input** ({attr}`ParameterSource.COMMANDLINE`),
614	2. **environment variable** named in `envvar=` or derived from `auto_envvar_prefix`
615	   ({attr}`ParameterSource.ENVIRONMENT`),
616	3. **`default_map` entry** matching the parameter name on the active {class}`Context`
617	   ({attr}`ParameterSource.DEFAULT_MAP`),
618	4. **parameter default** ({attr}`ParameterSource.DEFAULT`).
619	
620	The first source that produces a value wins. Environment variables and
621	`default_map` entries set to `Sentinel.UNSET` are skipped, so they fall through
622	to the next source rather than supplying `UNSET` to the function.
623	
624	If after the four sources above no explicit value was found (or only a
625	`default_map`/`default` value was) and the option declares `prompt=`, Click
626	prompts the user for one. The resulting value is recorded as
627	{attr}`ParameterSource.PROMPT`, which ranks above every source listed above
628	for arbitration purposes (see [Slot arbitration](#slot-arbitration)).
629	
630	### Slot arbitration
631	
632	Several options can target the same `name` to form a feature switch group. When
633	they do, only one option's value reaches the function. Arbitration applies
634	these rules, in order:
635	
636	1. **By source.** Whichever option resolved its value from the most explicit
637	   source wins, regardless of decorator order. Any command-line input beats any
638	   default, an environment variable beats a `default_map` entry, and so on.
639	2. **Within the default tier, explicit beats auto-derived.** An option that
640	   received an explicit `default=` keyword wins over one whose default came
641	   from `default` interpretation.
642	3. **Otherwise, last declared wins.** When all options in the group resolved
643	   from the same source and tier (all auto-derived defaults, or all explicit
644	   defaults), the option declared last in the source code keeps the slot.
645	
646	## Values from Environment Variables
647	
648	To pass in a value from a specific environment variable use `envvar`.
649	
650	```{eval-rst}
651	.. click:example::
652	
653	    @click.command()
654	    @click.option('--username', envvar='USERNAME')
655	    def greet(username):
656	       click.echo(f"Hello {username}!")
657	
658	.. click:run::
659	
660	    invoke(greet, env={'USERNAME': 'john'})
661	```
662	
663	If a list is passed to `envvar`, the first environment variable found is picked.
664	
665	```{eval-rst}
666	.. click:example::
667	
668	    @click.command()
669	    @click.option('--username', envvar=['ALT_USERNAME', 'USERNAME'])
670	    def greet(username):
671	       click.echo(f"Hello {username}!")
672	
673	.. click:run::
674	
675	    invoke(greet, env={'ALT_USERNAME': 'Bill', 'USERNAME': 'john'})
676	
677	```
678	
679	Variable names are:
680	 - [Case-insensitive on Windows but not on other platforms](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/aa9eb5f757ceff461e6e996f12c89e5d9b583b01/Lib/os.py#L777-L789).
681	 - Not stripped of whitespace and should match the exact name provided to the
682	   `envvar` argument.
683	
684	For flag options, there are two concepts to consider: the activation of the flag
685	driven by the environment variable, and the value of the flag if it is
686	activated.
687	
688	The values read from environment variables are always strings and will require
689	extra processing. We need to transform these strings into boolean values that
690	will determine if the flag is activated or not.
691	
692	Here are the rules used to parse environment variable values for flag options:
693	   - `true`, `1`, `yes`, `on`, `t`, `y` are interpreted as activating the flag
694	   - `false`, `0`, `no`, `off`, `f`, `n` are interpreted as deactivating the
695	     flag
696	   - The presence of the environment variable without value is interpreted as
697	     deactivating the flag
698	   - Empty strings are interpreted as deactivating the flag
699	   - Values are case-insensitive, so the `True`, `TRUE`, `tRuE` strings are all
700	     interpreted as activating the flag
701	   - Values are stripped of leading and trailing whitespace before being
702	     interpreted, so the `" True "` string is transformed to `"true"` and thus
703	     activates the flag
704	   - If the flag option has a `flag_value` argument, passing that value in the
705	     environment variable will activate the flag, in addition to all the cases
706	     described above
707	   - Any other value is interpreted as deactivating the flag
708	
709	```{caution}
710	For boolean flags with a pair of values, the only recognized environment variable is the one provided to the `envvar` argument.
711	
712	So an option defined as `--flag/--no-flag`, with an `envvar="FLAG"` parameter, there is no magical `NO_FLAG=<anything>` variable that is recognized. Only the `FLAG=<anything>` environment variable is recognized.
713	```
714	
715	If the flag is activated, its value is set to `flag_value`. Otherwise, the value
716	defaults to `None`.
717	
718	## Multiple Options from Environment Values
719	
720	As options can accept multiple values, pulling in such values from
721	environment variables (which are strings) is a bit more complex. Click handles
722	this by deferring customization of the behavior to the `type`. For both
723	`multiple` and `nargs` with values other than
724	`1`, Click will invoke the {meth}`ParamType.split_envvar_value` method to
725	perform the splitting.
726	
727	The default implementation for all types is to split on whitespace. The
728	exceptions to this rule are the {class}`File` and {class}`Path` types
729	which both split according to the operating system's path splitting rules.
730	On Unix systems like Linux and OS X, the splitting happens on
731	every colon (`:`), and for Windows, splitting on every semicolon (`;`).
732	
733	```{eval-rst}
734	.. click:example::
735	
736	    @click.command()
737	    @click.option('paths', '--path', envvar='PATHS', multiple=True,
738	                  type=click.Path())
739	    def perform(paths):
740	        for path in paths:
741	            click.echo(path)
742	
743	    if __name__ == '__main__':
744	        perform()
745	
746	.. click:run::
747	
748	    import os
749	    invoke(perform, env={"PATHS": f"./foo/bar{os.path.pathsep}./test"})

158	## Showing Defaults
159	
160	To control the appearance of defaults pass `show_default`.
161	
162	```{eval-rst}
163	.. click:example::
164	
165	    @click.command()
166	    @click.option('--n', default=1, show_default=False, help='number of dots')
167	    def dots(n):
168	        click.echo('.' * n)
169	
170	.. click:run::
171	    invoke(dots, args=['--help'])
172	```
173	
174	For single option boolean flags, the default remains hidden if the default value is False, even if show default is set to true.
175	
176	```{eval-rst}
177	.. click:example::

179	    @click.command()
180	    @click.option('--n', default=1, show_default=True)
181	    @click.option("--gr", is_flag=True, show_default=True, default=False, help="Greet the world.")
182	    @click.option("--br", is_flag=True, show_default=True, default=True, help="Add a thematic break")
183	    def dots(n, gr, br):
184	        if gr:
185	            click.echo('Hello world!')
186	        click.echo('.' * n)
187	        if br:
188	            click.echo('-' * n)
189	
190	.. click:run::
191	   invoke(dots, args=['--help'])
192	```
193	
194	## Showing Environment Variables
195	
196	To control the appearance of environment variables pass `show_envvar`.

202	    @click.option('--username', envvar='USERNAME', show_envvar=True)
